questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin
questions.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at the origin?
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
questions.problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4(1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$

questions.problem:
The Cartesian equation of the circle defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4,\,0\le \theta <2\pi 
$$

is given by

$(x\,+$
{{field-1}}$)^{2}+(y\,-$
{{field-2}}$)^{2}=$
{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+3}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{5} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-4)^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-4)^{2}}{25} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ (x+3)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation is $(x+3)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=25.$

questions.problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+2}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+3}{3} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+3)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+3)^{2}}{9} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ (x+2)^{2}+(y+3)^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x+2)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=9.$

questions.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & ={(\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{25}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & ={(\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{25}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{25}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{25}{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{25}{4}(1) \\  & =\frac{25}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{25}{4}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-5}{4} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{16} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{4} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-5)^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ (x-5)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x-5)^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, as shown below. Construct a set of parametric equations, defined for $\theta\in[0,2\pi),$ that traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(2,0).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14038487/assets/156d160267551e9dbf4db42b14b1e0dbb46ab658a836a760cf31a42eb89662d3.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$ centered at  the origin are

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r,0).$

In our case, the radius is $r = 2.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=2\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point
canonical_examples.problem: Construct a set of parametric equations, defined for $\theta\in[0,2\pi),$ that generates a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(4,6).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x= r\cos\theta+a,\quad y=r\sin\theta+b,\quad  \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(4,6).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=2\cos\theta+4,\quad y=2\sin\theta+6,\quad\theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14038487/assets/f44fad12ad1f7d465423f92258caae38e0c536153ba2c3c3a6de573061c69993.png)

The quarter-circle above is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x = 6\cos\theta, \qquad y = 6\sin\theta.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

In our case, the radius $r = 6.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=6\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-circle, we associate the parameter $\theta$ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14038487/assets/4bd384e2b1a9d0568617ddbfd5ac7dbe9630882b45c40d7912f4809a6e0be551.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta$ to $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right],$ we get the required quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-circle are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=6\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right].
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=3\cos\theta + 2,\quad y=3\sin\theta - 4, \quad 0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta.$ We can do this using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+4}{3} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2}+(y+4)^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x-2)^2 + (y+4)^2 = 9.$
